entities.summary:
Job is the central figure of the Book of Job, one of the most philosophically profound texts in the Hebrew Bible and world literature. Described as a righteous man living in the land of Uz, he suffers catastrophic losses — children, wealth, and health — as the result of a wager between God and the Adversary (ha-Satan), who challenges whether Job's piety is disinterested or merely self-serving. Job's story poses the ancient problem of theodicy: why do the innocent suffer?

The book interweaves a prose prologue and epilogue framing a series of poetic dialogues between Job and three friends (Eliphaz, Bildad, Zophar) who argue that his suffering must be punishment for sin. Job rejects this explanation, insisting on his innocence and demanding a direct hearing from God. A fourth voice, Elihu, attempts mediation. God eventually speaks from the whirlwind in one of the most celebrated passages in ancient literature — not answering Job's questions directly but overwhelming him with the incomprehensible vastness of creation.

The Book of Job has shaped Jewish, Christian, and Islamic theology, philosophy, and literature for millennia. Its influence extends from the Psalms to the rabbinical tradition, from the desert fathers to Aquinas, from Milton's Satan to Kafka, Dostoevsky, and Wiesel. The World Council of Churches has identified it as the Bible's most challenging theodicy; scholars date the book's composition between the 7th and 4th centuries BCE, though it draws on ancient Near Eastern wisdom traditions.
